Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
236 PM EDT Wed Sep 16 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 235 PM EDT Wednesday...

No significant changes.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 235 PM EDT Wednesday...

1. A few showers tomorrow before dry weather finishes out the 
week. 

2. Chances for showers trending down this weekend, but 
remaining seasonable cool.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 235 PM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: An area of rain will attempt to move into the region 
tomorrow into tomorrow night as isentropic lift occurs on a warm 
front. Uncertainty still exists on how far the northern extent will 
make it, with the CAMs generally split. Some members like the HRRR 
favor a surface low beginning to develop and bring the rain up into 
central and northern Vermont, while others like the NAM keep it more 
of an open wave and restrict precipitation to southern Vermont. 
Therefore, a period of rain is likely in southern Vermont tomorrow 
afternoon and evening while it is more of a chance for rain farther 
north. The rain will be stratiform and light, with expected amounts 
up to around a quarter inch in southern Vermont. Surface high 
pressure builds down from Canada Friday into Friday night, bringing 
a much cooler and drier airmass. By Friday night, temperatures 
should fall into the 40s and 30s, with patchy frost possible in the 
colder hollows of the Adirondacks and Northeast Kingdom. Highs will 
be cooler on Saturday with temperatures topping out in the 60s with 
low humidity.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Following a washed out cold front by the end of the work 
week, trends have continued to move towards the ECMWF solution 
keeping most, if not all, precipitation south of the area Saturday 
night. The baroclinic zone responsible for the area of potential 
showers will be draped more over central and southern New York with 
better forcing southwest of our region. That said, model solutions 
Sunday into Monday denote a subtle redevelopment of a surface low in 
southern New England which could bring some light shower chances to 
mainly southern Vermont. Ensemble variations denote less than 40% of 
members with rain over our region Saturday-Sunday. Our flow pattern 
will remain confluent through the weekend, so any precipitation that 
does materialize will likely be short lived. Model solutions begin 
to vary by early next week in terms of precipitation chances. An 
upper level high over the Great Lakes will set up a dry corridor 
from the Great Lakes into northern New England, while a moisture 
axis over the Mid Atlantic attempts to push north. Model uncertainty 
in how much dry air there is will determine if moisture and 
associated shower potential are able to penetrate northward into our 
region, or if dry subsident air keeps our shower chances shunted to 
the south. Trends have shifted the high a bit east, more centered 
over our north early next week, which bodes some better confidence 
in a drier start to next week. Regardless, zonal northwesterly flow 
will keep our temperatures through the weekend into early next week 
on the seasonably cool side with highs fairly consistent in the mid 
to upper 60s, and lows in the low to mid 40s, with some cold hollows 
hovering about the upper 30s. A sign of the changing seasons, our 
upper air pattern in the ensembles is beginning to show hints of 
some CAD by Tuesday, as the high to our north shifts further east, 
which would lead to some cool trapped air east of the Greens by mid 
next week. Sky conditions favor mainly cloudy conditions through the 
extended.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 18Z Thursday...Calm weather is expected to continue for the
next 12 or so hours before a frontal system begins to move through
the area. Most sites are seeing ceilings 3500-5000ft agl, with
terrain influences leading to high MVFR cigs at SLK. Ceilings will
turn more scattered and rise to 5000-7000ft agl this afternoon.
Winds will calm over the next few hours, as they turn more west-
northwest by 20-22Z. The challenging aspect to this forecast will be
any localized fog and low ceilings potential. Beyond 00Z, clouds
will hover and gradually lower back towards 3000-4000ft agl, with
models varying on how low ceilings go. Observations upstream denote
IFR low stratus over northern Indiana which is part of our
approaching air mass. However, as a cold front slides east tonight,
the eastward extend of the frontal passage will determine how north
these low ceilings get. Subsequently, a further east passage, may
allow for some clearing at EFK, enough for brief patchy fog.
Confidence for fog tonight is relatively low with expectations for
low stratus ceilings, in addition to a detachment from rain.
Ceilings will trend towards MVFR 1500-2500ft agl outside of MSS/EFK
after sunrise tomorrow, with shower chances at the end of this TAF
period. Winds remain light and variable tomorrow.
